options.option_text: Currents

questions.explanation: Tides are very long-period waves that move through the oceans in response to the gravitational forces exerted by the moon and sun. They originate in the oceans and progress toward the coastlines where they appear as the regular rise and fall of the sea surface.

questions.stem: Which bay holds the distinction of recording the world's highest tidal range, sometimes exceeding 16 metres between high and low tide?

options.option_text: Bay of Bengal, between eastern India and Myanmar
Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
Hudson Bay, a large body of water in northern Canada
Gulf of Carpentaria, in far northern Australia

questions.explanation: The Bay of Fundy in Canada regularly records tidal ranges of 14–17 m — the highest on Earth — due to tidal resonance and a funnel-shaped geometry. Hudson Bay is a common distractor but has a very modest tidal range of under 4 m. Bay of Bengal is associated with storm surges and tidal bores (Hooghly), not extreme range.

questions.stem: A coastal location that experiences exactly ONE high tide and ONE low tide within a single lunar day (≈24 h 50 min) is classified under which tidal regime?

options.option_text: Semi-diurnal tidal pattern with two equal peaks daily
Mixed tidal pattern with two unequal tidal peaks per day
Diurnal tidal pattern with a single complete daily cycle
Perigean tidal pattern occurring near the Moon's perigee

questions.explanation: Diurnal tides show one high and one low per lunar day and are common along parts of the Gulf of Mexico and South-East Asia. Semi-diurnal tides (e.g., Atlantic coasts) yield two nearly equal highs per day. Mixed tides give two highs of unequal height. Perigean is not a tidal regime classification but refers to tidal intensity when the Moon is at perigee.

questions.stem: When the Moon reaches its closest orbital point to Earth (perigee) and simultaneously occupies a new or full-moon phase, the resulting unusually high tides are specifically termed:

options.option_text: Apogean neap tides, caused by maximum lunar distance
Perigean spring tides, amplified by the Moon's orbital closeness
Proximal tidal surges driven by Earth-Sun gravitational alignment
Syzygy tides created solely by Earth-Sun gravitational coupling

questions.explanation: Perigean spring tides occur when two amplifying factors coincide: syzygy (Sun-Earth-Moon alignment giving spring tides) AND perigee (Moon at closest approach, ~356,500 km). This combination can push tides 20–25% higher than average spring tides and is associated with coastal flooding events. Apogean tides are the opposite — Moon at its farthest, producing subdued tides.

questions.stem: In tidal oceanography, an 'amphidromic point' is precisely defined as which of the following?

options.option_text: The ocean zone recording the maximum global tidal range
A fixed oceanic point where the tidal range is nearly zero
The deepest ocean trench where tidal forces are most amplified
A coastal headland where tidal bores regularly develop

questions.explanation: An amphidromic point is a nodal point in the ocean where the tidal range is effectively zero, and around which cotidal lines rotate like the hands of a clock (due to Coriolis effect and basin geometry). The North Sea contains several well-mapped amphidromic points. Students confuse it with areas of maximum tidal range — which is the exact opposite.

questions.stem: The Sun's tide-generating force on Earth's oceans is approximately what fraction of the Moon's tide-generating force, despite the Sun's vastly greater mass?

options.option_text: Roughly equal at 95–100% of the lunar tidal force
About 46% — less than half of the Moon's tidal pull
Around 70% — substantially close to the lunar tidal force
Merely 10–15% — negligible compared to the lunar pull

questions.explanation: Tidal force depends on the inverse cube of distance, not just mass. Although the Sun is ~27 million times more massive than the Moon, it is ~390 times farther away. This reduces its tidal force to roughly 46% of the Moon's. This is why the Moon dominates tidal patterns. Option C (70%) is a common over-estimate; 10–15% drastically understates solar influence, which is clearly visible during spring and neap tide cycles.

questions.stem: The Bay of Fundy's extraordinary tidal range of up to 17 m is primarily attributed to which specific oceanographic mechanism, beyond mere funnel-shaped coastal geometry?

options.option_text: Coriolis force deflecting all Atlantic tidal surges toward the bay
Tidal resonance, as the bay's natural oscillation period matches the semi-diurnal tidal cycle
Submarine volcanic uplift regularly displacing large water volumes
Density-driven thermohaline circulation concentrating surface water at the bay head

questions.explanation: The Bay of Fundy has a natural resonant period of approximately 12.4 hours, which closely matches the semi-diurnal tidal period of ~12.42 hours. This near-perfect resonance causes each incoming tidal wave to reinforce the previous oscillation, progressively amplifying tidal heights — analogous to pushing a swing in sync. The funnel shape contributes but is secondary. Option A (Coriolis) influences tidal rotation patterns globally but does not specifically amplify Bay of Fundy tides to this extreme.

questions.stem: Tidal friction progressively transfers angular momentum from Earth's axial rotation to the Moon's orbital motion. Which pair of long-term consequences does this process produce?

options.option_text: Earth's day shortens and the Moon gradually spirals inward toward Earth
Earth's day lengthens slowly and the Moon recedes from Earth over geological time
The Moon's axial tilt increases, eventually reversing its present tidal lock
Earth's rotational axis tilts further, permanently redistributing global tidal energy

questions.explanation: Tidal friction acts as a braking force on Earth's spin, causing the length of day to increase by ~1.4 milliseconds per century. Conservation of angular momentum requires the Moon to gain orbital energy and move to a higher orbit — receding at ~3.8 cm/year (confirmed by lunar laser ranging). Option A is the exact inverse — a common misconception conflating orbital and rotational mechanics. Option C confuses tidal locking (Moon already tidally locked) with its future disruption.
